The uniform-weights Bayes factor

Source: R/bf_uniform_weights.R
bf_uniform_weights.Rd

A researcher has coded the evidence into two counts: y_W observations support the working theory and y_R support a single rival. One model underlies every Bayes factor in this package. Each observation supports the working theory with probability \(\theta\), the share of the evidence that supports it. The working theory claims \(\theta > 1/2\) and the rival claims \(\theta \le 1/2\).

Usage

bf_uniform_weights(y_W, y_R, omega = 1)

Arguments

y_W

Non-negative whole number. Count, or summed weight, of observations supporting the working theory.

y_R

Non-negative whole number. Count, or summed weight, of observations supporting the rival.

omega

Positive number. The bias factor: how many times as likely the search was to find a pro-working-theory observation as a pro-rival one. Default 1, an unbiased search.

Value

A length-1 numeric: the Bayes factor in favor of the working theory.

Details

Each claim is a range of shares rather than one share, so neither gives a probability for the counts on its own. This function averages the binomial probability of the counts over each theory's range, giving every share in a range the same weight, and divides the working theory's average by the rival's. At nine observations for the working theory and three for the rival the two averages are 0.14675 and 0.00710, and the Bayes factor is 20.67. bf_worst_case() keeps the same numerator and evaluates the rival at a share of one half instead.

The paper's rule sets the rival aside, at least provisionally, when this value is 20 or more and the worst-case value is above 1. If every share from zero to one half is equally likely, this value averages exactly one over the counts the rival's claim could produce, so a researcher who follows the rule is misled at most one time in twenty on average over those shares, though not at every share.

Closed form

With \(N = y_W + y_R\) and \(S = \sum_{j=0}^{y_W} \binom{N+1}{j}\), the value is \(S / (2^{N+1} - S)\) (supplement, thm-closed-form). The function computes the same number as the ratio of the posterior masses above and below one half under a Beta\((y_W + 1, y_R + 1)\) distribution, which is what the equal weights on two equally wide ranges reduce to.

A biased search

A search omega times as likely to find a pro-working-theory observation as a pro-rival one turns a share \(\theta\) of the evidence into a share \(q = \omega\theta / (\omega\theta + 1 - \theta)\) among the observations found. Under bias the function puts \(q\) in place of \(\theta\) inside the binomial probability, keeps the equal weights on \(\theta\), and integrates. Granting more bias lowers the value. sens_bias() finds the bias at which the value falls to 20.

Weights on observations

A researcher who counts one observation as worth several routine ones gives it a whole-number weight and passes the summed weights as the counts: a memo weighted at ten among nine pro-working-theory observations gives bf_uniform_weights(18, 3), which is 2,337. These weights on observations are a different object from the weights on shares that bf_rescaled() takes.

See also

bf_worst_case() for the other Bayes factor from the same model; bf_rescaled() for weights on shares other than the uniform; bf_uniform_weights_finite() for documents read from an archive of known size; sens_bias() and sens_coding() for the sensitivity analyses.

Examples

# The paper's running example: nine observations support the working
# theory, three support the rival.
bf_uniform_weights(9, 3)
#> [1] 20.67196

# A search twice as likely to find pro-working-theory evidence.
bf_uniform_weights(9, 3, omega = 2)
#> [1] 2.854813

# The smoking-gun memo counted as ten observations.
bf_uniform_weights(18, 3)
#> [1] 2336.962
